source.title: Implicit to Explicit Entropy Regularization: Benchmarking ViT Fine-tuning under Noisy Labels
source.authors: Maria Marrium; Arif Mahmood; Mohammed Bennamoun

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests performance under controlled label corruption and measures prediction entropy, but does not test fitting completely random labels or training error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark results for symmetric and asymmetric label noise, but does not report training error. It does not test completely random labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, training time for random versus true labels, regularization ablations, or the order in which real and noisy labels are learned. Table II supplies the extracted test-accuracy series; cited findings are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The symmetric-noise sweeps test V4's prediction that test error increases with label corruption in a new setting: pretrained ViT fine-tuning. They do not establish perfect training-set fitting or memorization. Prediction entropy and comparisons of fine-tuning costs do not test the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but abbreviated. The authors conclude that full fine-tuning is more vulnerable to noisy labels than linear probing, extreme noise can substantially degrade ViT performance, existing NLL methods implicitly reduce prediction entropy, and explicit entropy regularization generally improves robustness. These are conclusions about noisy-label generalization, not demonstrated random-label memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Pre-trained ViT fine-tuning under synthetic and real-world label noise; evaluates test accuracy and prediction entropy, rather than fitting fully random labels and measuring training error.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, backbone, fine-tuning technique, loss function, noise type and rate, and entropy-regularization weight affect reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction entropy generally decreases over training, and the authors associate entropy reduction with validation/test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prediction entropy decreases during the tested noisy-label fine-tuning runs; this does not identify whether real patterns precede noise memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: ViTs outperform the compared CNNs under noisy labels, and explicit entropy regularization generally improves noisy-label test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretrained representations, fine-tuning choices, and entropy regularization affect robustness to label noise in the tested benchmarks.

record.problems: Extracted label-noise results report test accuracy but not training error, so they do not establish whether the models fit corrupted training labels. The selected CE series covers one backbone and fine-tuning method, and symmetric corruption only through η=0.8. The authors' abstract and conclusion summarize broad improvements, while several table entries show condition-dependent differences; no run-level details beyond reported uncertainty are supplied.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many separate conditions, models, losses, and datasets in Tables I–XX. To keep the record focused on the tested noise-degradation version, extracted a CE series for ViT-B/16 with MLP-3 across clean and symmetric noise rates in Table II; other losses, backbones, fine-tuning methods, asymmetric-noise conditions, aggregate comparisons, entropy measurements, and explicit-entropy-regularization results were not extracted because they do not directly test the versions' stated outcomes.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions. Figure 3(c) compares fine-tuning techniques instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fitting throughout the corruption sweep, memorization of corrupted labels, and the endpoint at completely random labeling; symmetric noise is evaluated only through η=0.8.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them impairs true-label generalization.
Separate learning trajectories for real patterns and corrupted labels, and their relative learning order. Entropy trajectories cannot establish this.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope verdict: missing training accuracy and an untested random-label endpoint are untested parts, not observed failures. The selected values match Table II, although its MNIST CE series conflicts with Table XII. Symmetric noise flips labels only to incorrect classes; η is not identical to the fraction replaced by independently uniform labels. Other reported condition families are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling condition, training error, or chance-level test error for that condition.
No random-label versus true-label training-time comparison or convergence-time sweep by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input conditions.

Training-set fit or perfect training accuracy is not reported; symmetric noise is tested only through η=0.8, not all labels corrupted; the study does not establish that remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
No weight-decay, dropout, or data-augmentation ablation testing random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Entropy is measured across training epochs, but the paper does not compare learning order for real-label patterns versus noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: ViT-B/16 with frozen backbone, MLP-3 fine-tuning and CE; symmetric noise from clean through η=0.8 on MNIST
relationships.reason: R1–R5 show monotonically declining test accuracy, 98.83% to 91.80%; this supports only the test-error component, with conflicting MNIST values in Table XII.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined monotonically from 98.83% to 91.80%, although another table reported conflicting MNIST values.

relationships.condition: ViT-B/16 with frozen backbone, MLP-3 fine-tuning and CE; symmetric noise from clean through η=0.8 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
relationships.reason: R6–R15 show monotonically declining test accuracy, 96.80% to 32.03% and 86.12% to 36.71%; this supports the test-error component without establishing training-set memorization.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined monotonically from 96.80% to 32.03% on CIFAR-10 and from 86.12% to 36.71% on CIFAR-100.
